Stochastic Thermodynamics of Score Matching in Diffusion Models

Xuehao Ding Email: xding@flatironinstitute.org Affiliation: Flatiron Institute, Simons Foundation    H. T. Quan Email: htquan@pku.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Physics, Peking University Affiliation: Collaborative Innovation Center of Quantum Matter, Peking University Affiliation: Frontiers Science Center for Nano-optoelectronics, Peking University    Yuhai Tu Email: ytu@flatironinstitute.org Affiliation: Flatiron Institute, Simons Foundation
Abstract

Score-based diffusion models are a powerful class of generative AI systems capable of sampling from complex, high-dimensional probability distributions. Their dynamics consist of a forward diffusion process that transforms data into noise and a learned reverse process that reconstructs data by reversing the probability flow. Here, we develop a stochastic thermodynamic framework for diffusion models and their score-matching objective. We introduce a trajectory-dependent quantity, time-asymmetry entropy production (TAEP), defined from the forward and reverse diffusion dynamics, and show that it obeys exact fluctuation theorems. Remarkably, Hyvärinen’s implicit score-matching kernel emerges naturally as a fluctuating component of TAEP, while the average TAEP is exactly proportional to the score-matching objective. We further show that fluctuations of TAEP quantify sampling unevenness and provide a thermodynamic measure of data-manifold coverage. These results yield a quantitative explanation for the superior sampling diversity of diffusion models and reveal a thermodynamic mechanism by which stochastic gradient descent favors flatter, more generalizable solutions. By uncovering the entropic nature of score matching, our work establishes fundamental statistical-mechanical principles underlying diffusion-based generative AI.

1 Main

The diffusion model Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) is a state-of-the-art generative machine learning framework with broad applications in computer vision, audio generation, natural language processing, and more. Mathematically, the diffusion model provides a general approach capable of learning the structure of sophisticated data distributions in high-dimensional spaces, e.g., the distribution of naturalistic images. Intuitively, the forward process continuously adds noise to the data sample until it becomes pure Gaussian noise. The learned reverse sampling process is expected to act as a denoiser at each time step to turn the noise back into a generated data sample. That is, the reverse process should reverse the arrow of time to evolve the Gaussian distribution into the target data distribution.

The original work on the diffusion model Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) was inspired by the Jarzynski equality Jarzynski (1997b) and the fluctuation theorem Seifert (2005), which conceptualize forward and backward trajectories of thermodynamic systems. Despite the fact that the vanilla diffusion model was formulated as a variational inference problem, subsequent efforts Song and Ermon (2019); Ho et al. (2020); Song et al. () demonstrated that the reverse sampling process could be understood as a reverse-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) Anderson (1982) and the objective function for training diffusion models could be reformulated via score matching Hyvärinen and Dayan (2005).

The SDE perspective allows diffusion models to be interpreted as stochastic physical systems and analyzed within the framework of nonequilibrium statistical physics. Recent studies have explored this direction from several angles, including entropy production Yu and Huang (2025), speed–accuracy trade-offs and optimal learning protocols Ikeda et al. (2025), and spontaneous symmetry breaking in reverse diffusion dynamics Biroli and Mézard (2023); Raya and Ambrogioni (2023); Biroli et al. (2024); Ambrogioni (2025). However, none of these works establishes a direct link between thermodynamic principles and the score-matching objective, the canonical objective for training diffusion models and a cornerstone of modern generative AI.

In this work, we develop a stochastic thermodynamic framework for diffusion models. Motivated by trajectory-based formulations of work Jarzynski (1997b); Sekimoto (2010) and entropy production (EP) Seifert (2005), we introduce time-asymmetry entropy production (TAEP), which we will show is a trajectory-based score-matching objective. After reviewing key concepts from stochastic thermodynamics, in particular path-integral representations of EP and fluctuation theorems, we formulate the forward and reverse diffusion processes using Langevin equations and derive explicit expressions for both fluctuating and average TAEP. We establish the fluctuation theorems for TAEP and demonstrate its fundamental connection to score matching. In the special case where the neural network represents an exact score field, TAEP directly quantifies the discrepancy between the generated and target distributions.

Our framework leads to two main consequences. First, the fluctuation theorem provides a thermodynamic explanation for the high sampling diversity and broad data-manifold coverage of diffusion models, linking these properties to fluctuations of TAEP. Second, a corollary of the fluctuation theorem predicts an architecture-agnostic positive relationship between SGD noise strength and loss-landscape curvature, suggesting that stochastic optimization naturally drives the score-matching objective toward flatter, and hence more generalizable, minima. Numerical experiments support these theoretical predictions.

2 Brief Review of Stochastic Thermodynamics

In this section, we briefly review key results in stochastic thermodynamics relevant to our work Seifert (2012); Esposito and Van den Broeck (2010a); Van den Broeck and Esposito (2015). Consider a small system in contact with a heat reservoir. The dynamics of the system are stochastic due to thermal fluctuations. In the continuous setting, the evolution of the probability distribution of the system state can be described by the Fokker-Planck equation:

∂p⁡(x,t)∂t=−∇⋅[μF(x)p(x,t)−μkBT∇p(x,t)],\frac{\partial p(x,t)}{\partial t}=-\nabla\cdot[\mu F(x)p(x,t)-\mu k_{B}T\nabla p(x,t)], (1)

where μ\mu is the mobility, F⁡(x)F(x) is the force, kBk_{B} is the Boltzmann constant, and TT is the temperature of the heat reservoir.

Consider a fixed time interval t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau], over which the probability distribution of the system evolves from p⁡(x,0)p(x,0) to p⁡(x,τ)p(x,\tau). The total entropy production of each trajectory x⁡([t])x([t]) satisfies the following relation Seifert (2005); Maes and Netočnỳ (2003).

Δ​st​o​t​[x⁡([t])]=kB​log⁡p⁡[x⁡([t])]p¯​[x¯​([t])],\Delta s_{tot}[x([t])]=k_{B}\log\frac{p[x([t])]}{\bar{p}[\bar{x}([t])]}, (2)

where pp is the forward probability density measure of trajectories with the initial distribution p⁡(x,0)p(x,0), p¯\bar{p} is the backward probability density measure under the same dynamics as the forward process but with the initial distribution p⁡(x,τ)p(x,\tau), and x¯​([t])\bar{x}([t]) denotes the time-reversed trajectory of x⁡([t])x([t]), i.e., x​(t)=x¯​(τ−t)x(t)=\bar{x}(\tau-t). The total EP can be decomposed into the EP of the system Δ​ss​y​s\Delta s_{sys} and the EP of the heat bath Δ​sb​a​t​h\Delta s_{bath}, which satisfy

Δ​st​o​t=Δ​ss​y​s+Δ​sb​a​t​h,\Delta s_{tot}=\Delta s_{sys}+\Delta s_{bath}, (3)
Δ​ss​y​s​[x⁡([t])]=(−kB​log⁡p⁡[x⁡(τ),τ])−(−kB​log⁡p⁡[x⁡(0),0]),\displaystyle\Delta s_{sys}[x([t])]=(-k_{B}\log p[x(\tau),\tau])-(-k_{B}\log p[x(0),0]), (4)
Δ​sb​a​t​h​[x⁡([t])]=kB​log⁡p⁡[x⁡([t])|x⁡(0)]p¯​[x¯​([t])|x​(τ)].\Delta s_{bath}[x([t])]=k_{B}\log\frac{p[x([t])|x(0)]}{\bar{p}[\bar{x}([t])|x(\tau)]}. (5)

The ensemble averages of these trajectory-level quantities agree with the standard macroscopic EPs:

⟨Δ​ss​y​s⟩=Δ​Ss​y​s,⟨Δ​sb​a​t​h⟩=Δ​Sb​a​t​h,⟨Δ​st​o​t⟩=Δ​St​o​t.\displaystyle\langle\Delta s_{sys}\rangle=\Delta S_{sys},\;\langle\Delta s_{bath}\rangle=\Delta S_{bath},\;\langle\Delta s_{tot}\rangle=\Delta S_{tot}. (6)

From equation (2), one can derive the following integral fluctuation theorem and detailed fluctuation theorem for total EP via path integration Van den Broeck and Esposito (2015).

⟨exp⁡(−Δ​st​o​tkB)⟩=1,\displaystyle\langle\exp(-\frac{\Delta s_{tot}}{k_{B}})\rangle=1, (7)
p⁡(Δ​st​o​t)p¯​(−Δ​st​o​t)=exp⁡(Δ​st​o​tkB).\displaystyle\frac{p(\Delta s_{tot})}{\bar{p}(-\Delta s_{tot})}=\exp(\frac{\Delta s_{tot}}{k_{B}}). (8)

Here, the probability measures of EP are defined as

p⁡(σ)=∫𝒟​x​([t])​δ​(σ−kB​log⁡p⁡[x⁡([t])]p¯​[x¯​([t])])​p​[x⁡([t])],\displaystyle p(\sigma)=\int\mathcal{D}x([t])\delta\left(\sigma-k_{B}\log\frac{p[x([t])]}{\bar{p}[\bar{x}([t])]}\right)p[x([t])], (9)
p¯​(σ)=∫𝒟​x¯​([t])​δ​(σ−kB​log⁡p¯​[x¯​([t])]p⁡[x⁡([t])])​p¯​[x¯​([t])].\displaystyle\bar{p}(\sigma)=\int\mathcal{D}\bar{x}([t])\delta\left(\sigma-k_{B}\log\frac{\bar{p}[\bar{x}([t])]}{p[x([t])]}\right)\bar{p}[\bar{x}([t])]. (10)

Applying Jensen’s inequality to equation (7) yields the second law of thermodynamics

Δ​St​o​t=⟨Δ​st​o​t⟩≥0.\Delta S_{tot}=\langle\Delta s_{tot}\rangle\geq 0. (12)

The detailed fluctuation theorem, equation (8), states that an entropy increase is exponentially more probable than an entropy decrease.

Aside from splitting the total EP into system EP and reservoir EP (equation (3)), an alternative way is to split the total EP into non-adiabatic EP and adiabatic EP, closely related to the concepts of excess heat and housekeeping heat Oono and Paniconi (1998); Hatano and Sasa (2001); Esposito and Van den Broeck (2010a); Esposito and Van den Broeck (2010b); Van den Broeck and Esposito (2010). Intuitively, the non-adiabatic EP is the extra EP relative to the corresponding adiabatic process. Thus, the non-adiabatic EP of an adiabatic process is zero. The non-adiabatic EP of each trajectory x⁡([t])x([t]) satisfies the following relation.

Δ​sn​a​[x⁡([t])]=kB​log⁡p⁡[x⁡([t])]p¯†​[x¯​([t])],\Delta s_{na}[x([t])]=k_{B}\log\frac{p[x([t])]}{\bar{p}^{\dagger}[\bar{x}([t])]}, (13)

where p¯†\bar{p}^{\dagger} denotes the probability density measure of the backward trajectory under the dual dynamics with the initial condition p⁡(x,τ)p(x,\tau). The force of the dual dynamics is given by

F†(x)=−F(x)+2kBT∇logps​t(x),\displaystyle F^{\dagger}(x)=-F(x)+2k_{B}T\nabla\log p^{st}(x), (14)

where ps​t​(x)p^{st}(x) denotes the stationary distribution of the forward dynamics, and the diffusion term of the dual dynamics is the same as that of the forward dynamics. Similarly to total EP, non-adiabatic EP also satisfies an integral fluctuation theorem and a detailed fluctuation theorem Esposito and Van den Broeck (2010a):

⟨exp⁡(−Δ​sn​akB)⟩=1,\displaystyle\langle\exp(-\frac{\Delta s_{na}}{k_{B}})\rangle=1, (15)
p⁡(Δ​sn​a)p¯†​(−Δ​sn​a)=exp⁡(Δ​sn​akB),\displaystyle\frac{p(\Delta s_{na})}{\bar{p}^{\dagger}(-\Delta s_{na})}=\exp(\frac{\Delta s_{na}}{k_{B}}), (16)

where the dual-reversed probability measure of EP is defined as

p¯†​(σ)=∫𝒟​x¯​([t])​δ​(σ−kB​log⁡p¯†​[x¯​([t])]p⁡[x⁡([t])])​p¯†​[x¯​([t])].\bar{p}^{\dagger}(\sigma)=\int\mathcal{D}\bar{x}([t])\delta\left(\sigma-k_{B}\log\frac{\bar{p}^{\dagger}[\bar{x}([t])]}{p[x([t])]}\right)\bar{p}^{\dagger}[\bar{x}([t])]. (17)

With a change of variables, equation (15) becomes the well-known Hatano-Sasa relation Hatano and Sasa (2001).

3 Time-asymmetry entropy production in diffusion models

3.1 Diffusion model described by Langevin equations

A diffusion model consists of a forward diffusion process and a reverse sampling process (Fig. 1). The forward process transforms a generically intractable data distribution into a tractable Gaussian distribution by adding noise to data samples. The reverse process has to be trained to evolve the Gaussian distribution back into the target data distribution by denoising corrupted samples.

We model the forward process of the diffusion model using a high-dimensional overdamped Langevin equation.

d​x=μ​F​(x)​d​t+2​μ​kB​T∘d​Wt,dx=\mu F(x)dt+\sqrt{2\mu k_{B}T}\circ dW_{t}, (18)

where t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau], x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denotes the corrupted data sample in the forward diffusion process, F⁡(x)∈ℝnF(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denotes the drift force, and Wt∈ℝnW_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is a Wiener process. Following the convention of stochastic thermodynamics, here we adopt Stratonovich’s stochastic calculus Sekimoto (2010). In the literature on diffusion models, the setting F⁡(x)=0F(x)=0 is termed variance-exploding, in which the variance of the distribution grows without bound. In contrast, F⁡(x)=−kB​Tσ2​xF(x)=-\frac{k_{B}T}{\sigma^{2}}x is termed variance-preserving with the stationary variance equal to σ2\sigma^{2}, which corresponds to an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.

The evolution of the probability distribution p⁡(x,t)p(x,t) is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation, equation (1), and p⁡(x,0)p(x,0) represents the target data distribution. The probability current of the forward process is given by

J(x,t)=p(x,t)[μF(x)−μkBT∇logp(x,t)].J(x,t)=p(x,t)[\mu F(x)-\mu k_{B}T\nabla\log p(x,t)]. (19)

The dynamics of the reverse sampling process can also be described by an overdamped Langevin equation, albeit non-autonomous Song et al. ():

d​x~=μ⁡[−F⁡(x~)+2​kB​T​sθ​(x~,t~)]​d​t~+2​μ​kB​T∘d​W~t,d\widetilde{x}=\mu[-F(\widetilde{x})+2k_{B}Ts_{\theta}(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t})]d\widetilde{t}+\sqrt{2\mu k_{B}T}\circ d\widetilde{W}_{t}, (20)

where t~∈[0,τ]\widetilde{t}\in[0,\tau], x~∈ℝn\widetilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denotes the intermediate denoised sample in the reverse process, sθ​(x~,t~)∈ℝns_{\theta}(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the denoising neural network with parameters θ\theta, W~t∈ℝn\widetilde{W}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the Wiener process in the reverse process. The only difference from the dual dynamics (equation 14) is that the stationary score is replaced by the denoising network. Let p~θ​(x~,t~)\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t}) denote the parameter-dependent probability distribution in the reverse process. Since the purpose of the reverse process is to transform the final distribution of the forward process into the data distribution, we naturally have the following.

p~θ​(x,0)=p⁡(x,τ).\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(x,0)=p(x,\tau). (21)

The probability current of the backward process is given by

J~θ(x~,t~)=p~θ(x~,t~)[−μF(x~)+2μkBTsθ(x~,t~)−μkBT∇logp~θ(x~,t~)].\displaystyle\widetilde{J}_{\theta}(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t})=\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t})[-\mu F(\widetilde{x})+2\mu k_{B}Ts_{\theta}(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t})-\mu k_{B}T\nabla\log\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t})]. (22)

When there exists a set of parameters θ∗\theta^{*} such that

sθ∗​(x,t)=∇log⁡p​(x,τ−t),s_{\theta^{*}}(x,t)=\nabla\log p(x,\tau-t), (23)

equation (20) becomes the reverse-time SDE proposed by Ref. Anderson (1982), which reverses the probability current of the forward process. That is,

J~θ∗​(x,t)=−J⁡(x,τ−t),p~θ∗​(x,t)=p⁡(x,τ−t).\widetilde{J}_{\theta^{*}}(x,t)=-J(x,\tau-t),\quad\widetilde{p}_{\theta^{*}}(x,t)=p(x,\tau-t). (24)

Thus, assuming that the expressivity of the network architecture is sufficient, the fully trained network sθ​(x,t)s_{\theta}(x,t) is expected to converge to the score ∇log⁡p​(x,τ−t)\nabla\log p(x,\tau-t) and θ∗\theta^{*} is the optimal set of parameters.

In the literature on diffusion models, the canonical objective function to minimize is the score-matching objective defined as the mean squared error of the estimated score integrated over time Song et al. (), which is

ℒS​M​(θ)≔∫0τ⟨‖sθ​(x,τ−t)−∇log⁡p​(x,t)‖2⟩x∼p⁡(x,t)​𝑑t.\mathcal{L}_{SM}(\theta)\coloneq\int_{0}^{\tau}\langle||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)-\nabla\log p(x,t)||^{2}\rangle_{x\sim p(x,t)}dt. (25)

Clearly, the optimum satisfies ℒS​M​(θ∗)=0\mathcal{L}_{SM}(\theta^{*})=0. In the following, we reveal the entropic nature of the score-matching objective.

3.2 Entropic nature of score matching and fluctuation theorems

We now introduce the trajectory-dependent time-asymmetry entropy production (TAEP) for diffusion models, analogous to the total and non-adiabatic entropy productions satisfying equations (2) and (13), respectively:

Δ​st​a​[x⁡([t])]=kB​log⁡p⁡[x⁡([t])]p~θ​[x¯​([t])],\Delta s_{ta}[x([t])]=k_{B}\log\frac{p[x([t])]}{\widetilde{p}_{\theta}[\bar{x}([t])]}, (26)

where p~θ\widetilde{p}_{\theta} denotes the trajectory density measure under the reverse sampling dynamics, equation (20). We emphasize that equation (26) is not a conventional Radon–Nikodym derivative, but rather the ratio between trajectory densities in the Onsager–Machlup sense, as commonly used in stochastic thermodynamics Lau and Lubensky (2007).

For a perfectly trained model, equation (24) implies

p⁡[x⁡([t])]=p~θ∗​[x¯​([t])],p[x([t])]=\widetilde{p}_{\theta^{*}}[\bar{x}([t])], (27)

so that the TAEP vanishes identically for every trajectory. In practice, however, the learned score field is only approximate. The TAEP therefore quantifies the time asymmetry between the trajectory densities in the forward evolution and the learned reverse dynamics, providing a trajectory-level measure of model error.

Next, we explicitly evaluate equation (26). Using the method developed in stochastic thermodynamics Chernyak et al. (2006); Lau and Lubensky (2007), we find (see the Supplement, Section I):

Δ​st​a​[x⁡([t])]=μ​kB2​T​∫0τ[l⁡(θ,x⁡(t),t)−l⁡(θ∗,x⁡(t),t)]​𝑑t\displaystyle\Delta s_{ta}[x([t])]=\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}[l(\theta;x(t),t)-l(\theta^{*};x(t),t)]dt (28)
+kB2​μ​kB​T∫0τ[sθ(x(t),τ−t)−sθ∗(x(t),τ−t)]⊤dWt,\displaystyle+k_{B}\sqrt{2\mu k_{B}T}\int_{0}^{\tau}[s_{\theta}(x(t),\tau-t)-s_{\theta^{*}}(x(t),\tau-t)]^{\top}dW_{t},
l(θ;x,t)≔||sθ(x,τ−t)||2+2∇⋅sθ(x,τ−t).l(\theta;x,t)\coloneq||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)||^{2}+2\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t). (29)

Importantly, l⁡(θ,x,t)l(\theta;x,t) is precisely Hyvärinen’s implicit score-matching kernel introduced in the original work on score matching Hyvärinen and Dayan (2005). The last term consists of the projection of the score estimation error onto the corrupting noise Song et al. (2020).

Employing the path-integral technique in stochastic thermodynamics Seifert (2005); Esposito and Van den Broeck (2010a); Maes and Netočnỳ (2003), one can show from equation (26) that the fluctuating TAEP obeys the integral and detailed fluctuation theorems:

⟨exp⁡(−Δ​st​akB)⟩=1,\displaystyle\langle\exp(-\frac{\Delta s_{ta}}{k_{B}})\rangle=1, (30)
p⁡(Δ​st​a)p~θ​(−Δ​st​a)=exp⁡(Δ​st​akB),\displaystyle\frac{p(\Delta s_{ta})}{\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(-\Delta s_{ta})}=\exp(\frac{\Delta s_{ta}}{k_{B}}), (31)

which constitute one of the central theoretical results of this work. Here, the backward probability measure of EP is defined as

p~θ​(σ)=∫𝒟​x¯​([t])​δ​(σ−kB​log⁡p~θ​[x¯​([t])]p⁡[x⁡([t])])​p~θ​[x¯​([t])].\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(\sigma)=\int\mathcal{D}\bar{x}([t])\delta\left(\sigma-k_{B}\log\frac{\widetilde{p}_{\theta}[\bar{x}([t])]}{p[x([t])]}\right)\widetilde{p}_{\theta}[\bar{x}([t])]. (32)

We numerically verify the integral fluctuation theorem in Fig. 2. Moreover, for diffusion models trained on natural-image datasets, we find that the evolution of the TAEP distribution during training closely mirrors the evolution of work or EP distributions in thermodynamic systems approaching the quasi-static limit (Fig. 3(a); see also Fig. 8 of Ref. Jarzynski (1997a)). This observation suggests a deep analogy between diffusion-model optimization and nonequilibrium thermodynamic relaxation.

We next evaluate the ensemble-averaged TAEP. Remarkably, the average TAEP is exactly proportional to the score-matching objective (see the Supplement, Section II):

Δ​St​a=⟨Δ​st​a⟩=μ​kB2​T​ℒS​M​(θ).\Delta S_{ta}=\langle\Delta s_{ta}\rangle=\mu k_{B}^{2}T\mathcal{L}_{SM}(\theta). (33)

Moreover, the TAEP rate is given by

d​St​ad​t=μ​kB2​T​⟨‖sθ​(x,τ−t)−∇log⁡p​(x,t)‖2⟩x∼p⁡(x,t),\frac{dS_{ta}}{dt}=\mu k_{B}^{2}T\langle||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)-\nabla\log p(x,t)||^{2}\rangle_{x\sim p(x,t)}, (34)

which coincides with the instantaneous score-matching objective.

As explicitly demonstrated in equations (28), (33), and (34), TAEP provides a novel trajectory-based formulation of the score-matching objective in diffusion models. As we show in Section 4, fluctuations of the trajectory TAEP play a crucial role in understanding the behavior and performance of diffusion-based generative models.

3.3 TAEP measures target-to-generated distribution mismatch

To understand the physical meaning of TAEP, we consider the case in which the neural network sθ​(x,τ−t)s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t) represents an exact score field:

sθ​(x,τ−t)=∇log⁡q​(x,t),s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)=\nabla\log q(x,t), (35)

where q⁡(x,t)q(x,t) is a time-dependent density governed by the dynamics of the same forward process as p⁡(x,t)p(x,t). It follows that q⁡(x,0)q(x,0) is the distribution of generated samples. Even though equation (35) is not generally true, it holds as a valid approximation in several scenarios including transfer learning, generalization, and when the trained model is near-optimal (see the Supplement, Section III).

In this case, we find (see the Supplement, Section III) that the trajectory TAEP is given by

Δ​st​a​[x⁡([t])]=kB​∫0τ∂νlog⁡q⁡[x⁡(t),t]p⁡[x⁡(t),t]∘d​xν,\Delta s_{ta}[x([t])]=k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\partial_{\nu}\log\frac{q[x(t),t]}{p[x(t),t]}\circ dx^{\nu}, (36)

where we adopt Einstein notation and covariant indices: ∂0≔∂t\partial_{0}\coloneq\partial_{t}, x0≔tx^{0}\coloneq t. It follows that the ensemble-averaged TAEP rate can be expressed as the familiar form of a sum over fluxes times forces:

d​St​ad​t=kB​∫𝒥ν​(x,t)​Nν​(x,t)​𝑑x,\frac{dS_{ta}}{dt}=k_{B}\int\mathcal{J}^{\nu}(x,t)N_{\nu}(x,t)dx, (37)
Nν=∂νlog⁡q⁡(x,t)p⁡(x,t),N_{\nu}=\partial_{\nu}\log\frac{q(x,t)}{p(x,t)}, (38)

where 𝒥≔(p,J)\mathcal{J}\coloneq(p,J) denotes the spacetime probability current, and NνN_{\nu} denotes the corresponding thermodynamic force. Mathematically, equations (37) and (38) reduce to the non-adiabatic EP rate when q⁡(x,t)q(x,t) is the stationary distribution of the forward dynamics Van den Broeck and Esposito (2010).

Importantly, in the limit τ→∞\tau\rightarrow\infty, the TAEP depends only on the initial condition:

Δst​a[x([t])]=kBlogp⁡[x⁡(0),0]q⁡[x⁡(0),0],ΔSt​a=kBDK​L[p(x,0)||q(x,0)],\Delta s_{ta}[x([t])]=k_{B}\log\frac{p[x(0),0]}{q[x(0),0]},\quad\Delta S_{ta}=k_{B}D_{KL}[p(x,0)||q(x,0)], (39)

which directly measures the discrepancy between the target and generated distributions.

4 Applications

In this section, we apply the integral fluctuation theorem to study the performance of diffusion models in terms of sampling diversity and learning dynamics. Our study reveals how the variance of the TAEP distribution characterizes sampling unevenness in diffusion models and how it is implicitly minimized by optimization. Furthermore, we show that in diffusion models, the SGD noise covariance is positively correlated with the Hessian of the objective function, thereby driving the optimization toward flatter minima.

4.1 Var(Δ​st​a)(\Delta s_{ta}) as a signature of diversity in generative sampling

In heat engines, average work and average entropy production define efficiency. However, assessing reliability requires knowing how much these fluctuating quantities vary Ding et al. (2018); Pietzonka and Seifert (2018). We can apply this same logic to diffusion models. The standard score-matching objective only measures average sample quality. In contrast, higher-order moments of the TAEP reveal sampling unevenness across the data distribution.

A prime example of uneven sampling is mode collapse Salimans et al. (2016), in which a model concentrates its probability on just a few data types and fails to generate diverse samples, leaving other valid data modes underrepresented. To show how the TAEP distribution detects and quantifies mode collapse, we tested diffusion models on 2D Gaussian mixtures. We constructed models with different levels of mode collapse by fitting them to biased datasets (see Methods). As shown in Fig. 2a, the TAEP distributions clearly reflect the severity of mode collapse (middle panel). Specifically, the variance, Var(Δ​st​a)(\Delta s_{ta}), increases as mode collapse gets worse (right panel). Remarkably, every single model still strictly obeys the fluctuation theorem (right panel). The same trend of increasing Var(Δ​st​a)(\Delta s_{ta}) with the severity of mode collapse is observed for increasing numbers of collapsed modes, as shown in Fig. 2b. While the mean TAEP, Δ​St​a\Delta S_{ta}, measures the average mismatch between the target and generated distributions, the variance provides further information on sampling heterogeneity (Fig. 2c).

We note that the above numerical results become analytically clear when considering the special case in which the neural network represents a score field (equation (35)) and τ→∞\tau\rightarrow\infty, as assumed in Section 3.3. It follows from equation (39) that the variance of the TAEP is given by the relative entropy variance:

Var​(Δ​st​a)=kB2​Varp⁡(x,0)​[log⁡p⁡(x,0)q⁡(x,0)],\text{Var}(\Delta s_{ta})=k_{B}^{2}\text{Var}_{p(x,0)}\left[\log\frac{p(x,0)}{q(x,0)}\right], (40)

a concept used in quantum information Li (2014).

The relative entropy variance complements KL divergence by tracking how unevenly errors are spread across samples, rather than just measuring the mean error level. Thus, Var​(Δ​st​a)\text{Var}(\Delta s_{ta}) can be used to distinguish between two diffusion models that have the exact same score-matching objective, i.e., even if their average first-order errors match, their second-order structures can be completely different (Fig. 2c). For example, one model might be consistently mediocre across the entire data space. The other model might fit some regions perfectly while completely missing others, which is what happens during mode collapse or other forms of nonuniform coverage. Interestingly, this exact trade-off between sample quality and diversity is a major focus of research on classifier-free diffusion guidance Ho and Salimans ().

We note that the first two moments of the TAEP can be related through the cumulant expansion of the integral fluctuation theorem, equation (30):

Δ​St​a=12​kB​Var​(Δ​st​a)+higher-order cumulants,\Delta S_{ta}=\frac{1}{2k_{B}}\text{Var}(\Delta s_{ta})+\text{higher-order cumulants}, (41)

which corresponds to the fluctuation-dissipation theorem for total EP when the higher-order cumulants are negligible, valid near equilibrium Jarzynski (1997b). Equation (41) indicates that the mean TAEP is proportional to the variance up to higher-order terms. Despite the higher-order correction, we provide a rigorous mathematical statement in terms of the asymptotic mean-variance relation as the mean approaches zero (see the Supplement, Section IV). This relation suggests that optimizations that reduce the score-matching objective also implicitly reduce the variance.

We numerically test our analytical results for diffusion models trained on natural images. The variance of the TAEP distribution tracks the coverage of the data manifold by generated samples, as defined in Ref. Naeem et al. (2020) (Fig. 3(b)). We further verify that the variance indeed decreases along with the mean during training (Fig. 3(c)), as detailed in Methods. Under the interpretation of the variance, the relationship between the first two moments of Δ​st​a\Delta s_{ta} naturally explains why diffusion models exhibit substantially milder mode collapse and better coverage of the full data distribution compared to earlier generative models, including GANs, VAEs, and autoregressive models Nichol and Dhariwal (2021); Dhariwal and Nichol (2021).

4.2 Landscape-dependent SGD Noise in Diffusion Models

For neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, the SGD noise is defined as the difference between the gradient of the per-sample or per-batch loss w.r.t. parameters and that of the mean loss. It has been found in multi-layer perceptron models that the covariance of SGD noise is positively correlated with the Hessian of the objective function w.r.t. model parameters, which characterizes the curvature of the loss landscape Jastrzebski et al. (2018). Specifically, in sharper directions of the loss landscape with larger Hessian eigenvalues, the SGD noise strength is also stronger. This loss-landscape-dependent anisotropic SGD noise is critical in biasing the optimization process toward finding flatter minima Feng and Tu (2021); Yang et al. (2023), which have been shown to have better generalization performance Feng et al. (2023). However, the positive correlation between the SGD noise covariance and the Hessian of the objective function has so far been shown only in simple model architectures Zhu et al. (2019); Li et al. (2020); Zhang et al. (2026).

For diffusion models and the score-matching objective, we note that the positive correlation between Hessian and SGD noise covariance is a direct consequence of the fluctuation theorem, agnostic of the model architecture. By taking the second-order gradient of equation (41) w.r.t. θ\theta, we obtain

𝐇θ​(Δ​St​a)=\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{\theta}(\Delta S_{ta})= 12​kB​Cov​(∇θΔ​st​a,∇θΔ​st​a)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2k_{B}}\text{Cov}(\nabla_{\theta}\Delta s_{ta},\nabla_{\theta}\Delta s_{ta}) (42)
+12​kB​Cov​(Δ​st​a,𝐇θ​(Δ​st​a))+higher-order terms,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2k_{B}}\text{Cov}(\Delta s_{ta},\mathbf{H}_{\theta}(\Delta s_{ta}))+\text{higher-order terms},

where 𝐇θ\mathbf{H}_{\theta} denotes the Hessian w.r.t. model parameters. According to equation (33), the LHS of the above equation is proportional to the Hessian of the score-matching objective. Since Δ​st​a\Delta s_{ta} is a per-trajectory loss, the first term of the RHS is the covariance of the SGD noise. The same statement also holds for the sample-wise covariance, as we show that the per-sample loss is a coarse-grained mean of the per-trajectory loss, so their variances exhibit a positive linear relationship (see the Supplement, Section V and Fig. S1).

We test the theoretical results using diffusion models trained on CIFAR-10 (see Methods). As shown in Fig. 4(a), the SGD noise covariance is positively correlated with the Hessian for parameters in various layers. The general trend across different layers of the network follows a power law with an exponent ∼1\sim 1, although the exponent within each layer is smaller (Fig. 4(b)). We also evaluate the overall strength of the SGD noise and the sharpness of the loss landscape characterized by the traces of the noise covariance and the Hessian, respectively, along the training trajectory. As shown in Fig. 4(c), the landscape-dependent SGD noise and sharpness of the loss landscape decrease with training. Our results demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that the SGD noise covariance is positively correlated with the Hessian in diffusion models, which can systematically bias the optimization of the score-matching objective toward flatter, more robust minima with better generalization.

5 Outlook

The diffusion model has two-level dynamics: 1. the dynamics of the forward and reverse processes; 2. the learning dynamics of the model during optimization. Thus, a natural next step is to discover the physical laws that govern the coupling between these two sets of dynamics. Since we find that the score-matching objective can be interpreted as entropy production, one may formulate the learning process under the general principle of minimal entropy production.

This work shows that the mathematical structure of the score-matching objective is very similar to that of non-adiabatic EP in classical stochastic thermodynamics, which has been studied for decades. Recent findings show that the concept of non-adiabatic entropy can be generalized to quantum physics Esposito et al. (2009); Horowitz and Sagawa (2014); Manzano et al. (2018). Therefore, our work also opens the possibility of constructing novel objective functions for generative AI models inspired by non-classical physics.

Stochastic thermodynamics provides a powerful framework for understanding fluctuations, irreversibility, and nonequilibrium processes. Despite substantial efforts, however, its real-world applications remain relatively limited. Our work offers a concrete example of how the concepts and principles of stochastic thermodynamics can be applied to practical scenarios.

In general, this work builds a conceptual bridge that allows statistical physicists to bring their expertise and rich toolbox to the field of generative AI. The results presented here suggest that this interface is a promising direction for future research, and we anticipate that further developments along these lines will yield increasingly significant discoveries.

Methods

1 Diffusion model on Gaussian mixture

1.1 Gaussian-mixture data distribution

We used a two-dimensional Gaussian-mixture model to test the interpretation of TAEP fluctuations as a diagnostic of sampling unevenness. The target distribution was an equally weighted mixture of K=8K=8 isotropic Gaussian components,

p⁡(x,0)=1K​∑k=1K𝒩⁡(x,mk,σ02​I2),x∈ℝ2.p(x,0)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{N}(x;m_{k},\sigma_{0}^{2}I_{2}),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. (43)

The component centers were placed uniformly on a circle,

mk=R(cos2​π​(k−1)K,sin2​π​(k−1)K),k=1,…,K.m_{k}=R\left(\cos\frac{2\pi(k-1)}{K},\sin\frac{2\pi(k-1)}{K}\right),\qquad k=1,\ldots,K. (44)

We used R=4R=4 and σ0=0.25\sigma_{0}=0.25. Samples were drawn directly from the Gaussian mixture without additional preprocessing or data augmentation.

1.2 Diffusion protocol and score-network architecture

We trained variance-preserving diffusion models following the standard DDPM procedure Ho et al. (2020). The noise schedule was linear in the variance-preserving SDE parameter, with βmin=0.1\beta_{\min}=0.1, βmax=20\beta_{\max}=20, and training times sampled uniformly from [10−3,1][10^{-3},1]. The time-dependent noise schedule can be absorbed into a monotone reparameterization of diffusion time to match the Langevin equation in the main text.

The score network was a multilayer perceptron sθ​(x,t):ℝ2×[0,1]→ℝ2s_{\theta}(x,t):\mathbb{R}^{2}\times[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}. The input consisted of the noisy sample xtx_{t} concatenated with a sinusoidal time embedding of tt. The network had three hidden layers of width 128128, SiLU nonlinearities, and a two-dimensional output. The same architecture was used for all controlled mode-collapse settings.

1.3 Optimization

The networks were trained with Adam using a learning rate of 10−310^{-3} and a batch size of 20482048. We clipped the global gradient norm at 1.01.0. Unless stated otherwise, each model was trained for 5×1045\times 10^{4} optimization steps. An exponential moving average (EMA) of the parameters was maintained during training and used for sampling and EP evaluation.

1.4 Controlled construction of mode-collapse models

To obtain controlled mode-collapse models, we trained diffusion models on biased Gaussian mixtures while evaluating all EP statistics relative to the uniform target distribution p0p_{0}. For a model with mm underrepresented modes, the training distribution was

q(m,ϵ)​(x,0)=∑k=1Kwk(m,ϵ)​𝒩​(x,mk,σ02​I2).q^{(m,\epsilon)}(x,0)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}^{(m,\epsilon)}\mathcal{N}(x;m_{k},\sigma_{0}^{2}I_{2}). (45)

The first mm modes were assigned probability ϵ\epsilon each,

wk(m,ϵ)=ϵ,k=1,…,m,w_{k}^{(m,\epsilon)}=\epsilon,\qquad k=1,\ldots,m, (46)

and the remaining K−mK-m modes shared the rest of the probability mass equally,

wk(m,ϵ)=1−m​ϵK−m,k=m+1,…,K.w_{k}^{(m,\epsilon)}=\frac{1-m\epsilon}{K-m},\qquad k=m+1,\ldots,K. (47)

For the single-mode-collapse experiment, we used m=1m=1 and varied ϵ=0.09,0.05,0.02,0.01,0.005\epsilon=0.09,0.05,0.02,0.01,0.005. For the multi-mode-collapse experiment, we fixed ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01 and varied m=1,…,5m=1,\ldots,5.

1.5 Trajectory-level TAEP evaluation

The TAEP of each trajectory was numerically evaluated following equation (28). The optimal score of the target distribution is available analytically. Under the variance-preserving forward process, the marginal distribution at time tt is still a Gaussian mixture,

p⁡(x,t)=1K​∑k=1K𝒩⁡(x,α¯​(t)​mk,vt​I2),p(x,t)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{N}\left(x;\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}(t)}\,m_{k},v_{t}I_{2}\right), (48)

where

vt=α¯​(t)​σ02+1−α¯​(t).v_{t}=\bar{\alpha}(t)\sigma_{0}^{2}+1-\bar{\alpha}(t). (49)

Here α¯​(t)\bar{\alpha}(t) is the cumulative signal factor of the variance-preserving diffusion process. Define

μk​(t)=α¯​(t)​mk\mu_{k}(t)=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}(t)}\,m_{k} (50)

and the posterior responsibility

rk​(x,t)=exp[−∥x−μk(t)∥2/(2vt)]∑j=1Kexp[−∥x−μj(t)∥2/(2vt)].r_{k}(x,t)=\frac{\exp\left[-\|x-\mu_{k}(t)\|^{2}/(2v_{t})\right]}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp\left[-\|x-\mu_{j}(t)\|^{2}/(2v_{t})\right]}. (51)

The exact optimal score is then

sθ∗​(x,t)=∇log⁡p​(x,t)=∑k=1Krk​(x,t)​[−x−μk​(t)vt].s_{\theta^{*}}(x,t)=\nabla\log p(x,t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_{k}(x,t)\left[-\frac{x-\mu_{k}(t)}{v_{t}}\right]. (52)

We used this analytical score as the optimal model in the trajectory-level EP calculation. Since the system is two-dimensional, the divergence term was evaluated exactly by automatic differentiation.

1.6 Analytical relative entropy variance

Equation (40) in the main text shows that in the exact-score-field and long-time limit,

Var⁡(Δ​stakB)=Varp⁡(x,0)​[log⁡p⁡(x,0)q⁡(x,0)].{\rm Var}\left(\frac{\Delta s_{\rm ta}}{k_{B}}\right)={\rm Var}_{p(x,0)}\left[\log\frac{p(x,0)}{q(x,0)}\right].

For well-separated Gaussian components with identical covariance and different mode weights, this reduces to a discrete mode-weight expression. If the target weights are uniform, pk=1/Kp_{k}=1/K, and the generated weights are wkw_{k}, then

Var⁡(Δ​stakB)≃1K​∑k=1K(log⁡1/Kwk−1K​∑j=1Klog⁡1/Kwj)2.{\rm Var}\left(\frac{\Delta s_{\rm ta}}{k_{B}}\right)\simeq\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\log\frac{1/K}{w_{k}}-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\log\frac{1/K}{w_{j}}\right)^{2}. (53)

For the controlled mm-mode-collapse construction,

w1=⋯=wm=ϵ,wm+1=⋯=wK=1−m​ϵK−m,w_{1}=\cdots=w_{m}=\epsilon,\qquad w_{m+1}=\cdots=w_{K}=\frac{1-m\epsilon}{K-m}, (54)

which gives

Var⁡(Δ​stakB)≃m⁡(K−m)K2​[log⁡1−m​ϵ(K−m)​ϵ]2.{\rm Var}\left(\frac{\Delta s_{\rm ta}}{k_{B}}\right)\simeq\frac{m(K-m)}{K^{2}}\left[\log\frac{1-m\epsilon}{(K-m)\epsilon}\right]^{2}. (55)

This analytical value was compared with the empirical variance measured from trained diffusion models.

2 Diffusion model on CIFAR-10

2.1 Diffusion protocol and model architecture

We trained a variance-preserving denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) on CIFAR-10, following the standard DDPM formulation of Ref. Ho et al. (2020). The forward process used T=1000T=1000 diffusion steps with a linear noise variance schedule βt\beta_{t} ranging from 10−410^{-4} to 2×10−22\times 10^{-2}. This time-dependent noise schedule can be absorbed into a monotone reparameterization of diffusion time to match the Langevin equation in the main text.

The score network was a U-Net operating on 32×3232\times 32 RGB images. The base channel width was 128, with channel multipliers (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2), two residual blocks per resolution level, and self-attention applied at the 16×1616\times 16 resolution. Timestep conditioning used sinusoidal embeddings followed by a two-layer multilayer perceptron of width 4×4\times the base channel dimension. Each residual block contained Group Normalization, SiLU nonlinearities, two 3×33\times 3 convolutions, and a linear projection of the timestep embedding; skip projections were used when the input and output channel dimensions differed. Downsampling was performed with learned stride-2 convolutions, whereas upsampling used nearest-neighbor interpolation followed by a 3×33\times 3 convolution. The bottleneck consisted of a residual block, an attention block, and a second residual block. The output head applied Group Normalization, SiLU, and a final 3×33\times 3 convolution back to three channels.

2.2 Dataset and preprocessing

We used the CIFAR-10 dataset for training and post-training analyses. Images were converted to tensors and linearly rescaled to the range [−1,1][-1,1] using channel-wise normalization with mean (0.5,0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5,0.5) and standard deviation (0.5,0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5,0.5). Training data were loaded with a batch size of 128128 and four data-loading workers, with incomplete final batches dropped.

2.3 Optimization

Models were trained for 500500 epochs with Adam using a learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}. Gradients were clipped to a global norm of 1.01.0 before each optimization step. An exponential moving average of the model parameters with decay 0.99990.9999 was maintained throughout training. Samples were generated from the EMA model.

2.4 Post-training analyses

In computing the TAEP for a trajectory, we substituted the finally trained model as the optimum, and estimated the divergence term using Hutchinson’s method Hutchinson (1989). We randomly sampled 10001000 trajectories for each model to estimate the variance of TAEP. The coverage metric is defined in Ref. Naeem et al. (2020). To study the geometry of the loss landscape, we computed Hessian matrices of the training loss with respect to selected subsets of parameters. Hessians for the selected parameter vector were accumulated over mini-batches. In separate calculations, we estimated the covariance of SGD noise by evaluating the gradient of the mini-batch loss with respect to the same parameter subsets and forming the centered empirical covariance matrix of these mini-batch gradients.

2.5 Structured parameter selection

We restricted the Hessian and SGD covariance analyses to structured subsets of ∼1000\sim 1000 parameters, for which exact dense Hessians remained computationally feasible. Parameter subsets were chosen in a manner that respected the internal organization of the network. For linear layers, we selected subsets of input and output nodes and retained the corresponding connections and biases. For convolutional layers, we selected subsets of input and output channels while retaining the full spatial kernel for each chosen channel pair. For attention blocks, we selected matched channel subsets across the query, key, and value projections. Group-normalization parameters were also selected.

3 Computational resources

Training and post-training analyses were performed in PyTorch on NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

I Fluctuating time-asymmetry entropy production

We discretize Eq. () using Stratonovich’s convention [25].

xn+1−xn=μ​F​(m)​Δ​t+2​μ​kB​T​Δ​t⋅zn,x_{n+1}-x_{n}=\mu F(m)\Delta t+\sqrt{2\mu k_{B}T\Delta t}\cdot z_{n}, (S1)

where m≔xn+1+xn2m\coloneq\frac{x_{n+1}+x_{n}}{2}, zn∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z_{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). Denote

Δ​xn=xn+1−xn,\Delta x_{n}=x_{n+1}-x_{n}, (S2)
h≔Δ​xn−μ​F​(m)​Δ​t,h\coloneq\Delta x_{n}-\mu F(m)\Delta t, (S3)

we have

p⁡(h|xn)=12​π⋅2​μ​kB​T​Δ​t​exp⁡(−‖h‖22⋅2​μ​kB​T​Δ​t).p(h|x_{n})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\cdot 2\mu k_{B}T\Delta t}}\exp\left(-\frac{||h||^{2}}{2\cdot 2\mu k_{B}T\Delta t}\right). (S4)

It follows that the forward transition probability is given by [25]

p⁡(xn+1|xn)=\displaystyle p(x_{n+1}|x_{n})= p⁡(h|xn)​det(∂h∂xn+1)\displaystyle p(h|x_{n})\det\left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{n+1}}\right) (S5)
=\displaystyle= p(h|xn)det(I−12μ∇F(m)Δt)\displaystyle p(h|x_{n})\det(I-\frac{1}{2}\mu\nabla F(m)\Delta t)
=\displaystyle= p(h|xn)[1−12μ∇⋅F(m)Δt+o(Δt)],\displaystyle p(h|x_{n})[1-\frac{1}{2}\mu\nabla\cdot F(m)\Delta t+o(\Delta t)],

where the last line uses Jacobi’s formula and Taylor expansion.

Similarly, we can calculate the transition probability of the reverse process from xn+1x_{n+1} to xnx_{n} at time t~=τ−t\widetilde{t}=\tau-t.

p~θ​(xn|xn+1;τ−t)=\displaystyle\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(x_{n}|x_{n+1};\tau-t)= 12​π⋅2​μ​kB​T​Δ​t​exp⁡(−‖−Δ​xn+μ​F​(m)​Δ​t−2​μ​kB​T​sθ​(m,τ−t)​Δ​t‖22⋅2​μ​kB​T​Δ​t)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\cdot 2\mu k_{B}T\Delta t}}\exp\left(-\frac{||-\Delta x_{n}+\mu F(m)\Delta t-2\mu k_{B}Ts_{\theta}(m,\tau-t)\Delta t||^{2}}{2\cdot 2\mu k_{B}T\Delta t}\right) (S6)
[1+12μ∇⋅F(m)Δt−μkBT∇⋅sθ(m,τ−t)Δt+o(Δt)].\displaystyle[1+\frac{1}{2}\mu\nabla\cdot F(m)\Delta t-\mu k_{B}T\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(m,\tau-t)\Delta t+o(\Delta t)].

Applying Taylor expansion to log⁡(1+x)\log(1+x) for x≪1x\ll 1, we have the following.

log⁡p⁡(xn+1|xn)p~θ​(xn|xn+1;τ−t)=\displaystyle\log\frac{p(x_{n+1}|x_{n})}{\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(x_{n}|x_{n+1};\tau-t)}= −‖Δ​xn−μ​F​(m)​Δ​t‖24​μ​kB​T​Δ​t+‖−Δ​xn+μ​F​(m)​Δ​t−2​μ​kB​T​sθ​(m,τ−t)​Δ​t‖24​μ​kB​T​Δ​t\displaystyle-\frac{||\Delta x_{n}-\mu F(m)\Delta t||^{2}}{4\mu k_{B}T\Delta t}+\frac{||-\Delta x_{n}+\mu F(m)\Delta t-2\mu k_{B}Ts_{\theta}(m,\tau-t)\Delta t||^{2}}{4\mu k_{B}T\Delta t} (S7)
+μkBT∇⋅sθ(m,τ−t)Δt−μ∇⋅F(m)Δt+o(Δt)\displaystyle+\mu k_{B}T\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(m,\tau-t)\Delta t-\mu\nabla\cdot F(m)\Delta t+o(\Delta t)
=\displaystyle= sθ​(m,τ−t)⊤​[Δ​xn−μ​F​(m)​Δ​t+μ​kB​T​sθ​(m,τ−t)​Δ​t]\displaystyle s_{\theta}(m,\tau-t)^{\top}[\Delta x_{n}-\mu F(m)\Delta t+\mu k_{B}Ts_{\theta}(m,\tau-t)\Delta t]
+μkBT∇⋅sθ(m,τ−t)Δt−μ∇⋅F(m)Δt+o(Δt).\displaystyle+\mu k_{B}T\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(m,\tau-t)\Delta t-\mu\nabla\cdot F(m)\Delta t+o(\Delta t).

By integrating along the trajectory, we obtain an expression of the TAEP for a trajectory x⁡([t])x([t]):

=\displaystyle= Δ​ss​y​s+kB​∫0τsθ​(x,τ−t)⊤​2​μ​kB​T​d​Wt\displaystyle\Delta s_{sys}+k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)^{\top}\sqrt{2\mu k_{B}T}dW_{t}
+μkB2T∫0τ[||sθ(x,τ−t)||2+2∇⋅sθ(x,τ−t)]dt−μkB∫0τ∇⋅F(x)dt,\displaystyle+\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}[||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)||^{2}+2\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)]dt-\mu k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\nabla\cdot F(x)dt,

where Δ​ss​y​s\Delta s_{sys} is defined as Eq. (), the third equality uses Eq. (), and the fourth equality converts the Stratonovich integral to the Itô integral.

We now expand the system entropy change as integrals.

Δ​ss​y​s=\displaystyle\Delta s_{sys}= −kB​Δ​log⁡p⁡(x,t)\displaystyle-k_{B}\Delta\log p(x,t) (S9)
=\displaystyle= −kB∫0τ[∇logp(x,t)]⊤∘dx−kB∫0τ∂log⁡p⁡(x,t)∂tdt\displaystyle-k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}[\nabla\log p(x,t)]^{\top}\circ dx-k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\frac{\partial\log p(x,t)}{\partial t}dt
=\displaystyle= −kB∫0τμ[∇logp(x,t)]⊤F(x)dt−kB∫0τ2​μ​kB​T[∇logp(x,t)]⊤dWt\displaystyle-k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\mu[\nabla\log p(x,t)]^{\top}F(x)dt-k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\sqrt{2\mu k_{B}T}[\nabla\log p(x,t)]^{\top}dW_{t}
−μkB2T∫0τ∇2logp(x,t)dt−kB∫0τ−∇⋅[μF(x)p(x,t)]+μkBT∇2p(x,t)p⁡(x,t)dt\displaystyle-\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}\nabla^{2}\log p(x,t)dt-k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\frac{-\nabla\cdot[\mu F(x)p(x,t)]+\mu k_{B}T\nabla^{2}p(x,t)}{p(x,t)}dt
=\displaystyle= μ​kB​∫0τ∇⋅F⁡(x)​𝑑t−kB​∫0τ2​μ​kB​T​[∇log⁡p​(x,t)]⊤​d​Wt\displaystyle\mu k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\nabla\cdot F(x)dt-k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\sqrt{2\mu k_{B}T}[\nabla\log p(x,t)]^{\top}dW_{t}
−μkB2T∫0τ[2∇2logp(x,t)+||∇logp(x,t)||2]dt,\displaystyle-\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}[2\nabla^{2}\log p(x,t)+||\nabla\log p(x,t)||^{2}]dt,

where the third equality converts the Stratonovich integral to the Itô integral and uses the Fokker-Planck equation. Combining Eqs. (S8)(S9), we finally obtain the expression of Δ​st​a\Delta s_{ta}.

Δ​st​a​[x⁡([t])]\displaystyle\Delta s_{ta}[x([t])] (S10)
=\displaystyle= kB​2​μ​kB​T​∫0τ[sθ​(x,τ−t)−∇log⁡p​(x,t)]⊤​d​Wt\displaystyle k_{B}\sqrt{2\mu k_{B}T}\int_{0}^{\tau}[s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)-\nabla\log p(x,t)]^{\top}dW_{t}
+μkB2T∫0τ[||sθ(x,τ−t)||2+2∇⋅sθ(x,τ−t)]dt−μkB2T∫0τ[||∇logp(x,t)||2+2∇2logp(x,t)]dt.\displaystyle+\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}[||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)||^{2}+2\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)]dt-\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}[||\nabla\log p(x,t)||^{2}+2\nabla^{2}\log p(x,t)]dt.

II Ensemble-averaged time-asymmetry entropy production

The last term of Eq. () is a martingale. Thus, the ensemble-averaged TAEP is given by

⟨Δ​st​a​[x⁡([t])]⟩\displaystyle\langle\Delta s_{ta}[x([t])]\rangle (S11)
=\displaystyle= μkB2T∫0τ∫p(x,t)[||sθ(x,τ−t)||2+2∇⋅sθ(x,τ−t)]dxdt\displaystyle\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}\int p(x,t)[||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)||^{2}+2\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)]dxdt
−μkB2T∫0τ∫p(x,t)[||∇logp(x,t)||2+2∇2logp(x,t)]dxdt.\displaystyle-\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}\int p(x,t)[||\nabla\log p(x,t)||^{2}+2\nabla^{2}\log p(x,t)]dxdt.

Using integration by parts and assuming that the boundary term is zero, we have

∫p(x,t)∇⋅sθ(x,τ−t)dx=−∫p(x,t)∇logp(x,t)⋅sθ(x,τ−t)dx,\displaystyle\int p(x,t)\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)dx=-\int p(x,t)\nabla\log p(x,t)\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)dx, (S12)
∫p(x,t)[||∇logp(x,t)||2+2∇2logp(x,t)]dx=−∫p(x,t)||∇logp(x,t)||2dx.\displaystyle\int p(x,t)[||\nabla\log p(x,t)||^{2}+2\nabla^{2}\log p(x,t)]dx=-\int p(x,t)||\nabla\log p(x,t)||^{2}dx. (S13)

Substituting Eqs. (S12)(S13) into Eq. (S11), we finally obtain

⟨Δ​st​a​[x⁡([t])]⟩=\displaystyle\langle\Delta s_{ta}[x([t])]\rangle= μ​kB2​T​∫0τ∫p⁡(x,t)​‖sθ​(x,τ−t)−∇log⁡p​(x,t)‖2​𝑑x​𝑑t\displaystyle\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}\int p(x,t)||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)-\nabla\log p(x,t)||^{2}dxdt (S14)
=\displaystyle= μ​kB2​T​ℒS​M​(θ).\displaystyle\mu k_{B}^{2}T\mathcal{L}_{SM}(\theta).

III Scenarios where the exact-score approximation is valid

In the following, we discuss several scenarios where the exact-score approximation, Eq. (), is valid.

  1. 1.

    Transfer learning, which is a machine learning paradigm that leverages knowledge acquired from a pre-trained source domain to enhance the learning efficiency and predictive performance of a model on a related but distinct task. Suppose that there is a dataset 𝒫\mathcal{P} with distribution p⁡(x,0)p(x,0) and a related dataset 𝒬\mathcal{Q} with distribution q⁡(x,0)q(x,0). Suppose that a diffusion model has been fully trained on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, i.e., Eq. () is satisfied. Now we want to train another diffusion model to learn the distribution of 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Instead of training from scratch, we start from the existing network to transfer knowledge about 𝒬\mathcal{Q} to the new diffusion model.

  2. 2.

    Generalization. Similarly to transfer learning, the model has been fully trained on the train set 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and now we test the model on the test set 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

  3. 3.

    Near-optimality. When θ\theta is in the neighborhood of the optimum θ∗\theta^{*}, sθ​(x,τ−t)s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t) can be well approximated as its projection onto the score-field space [24], which we denote by ∇log⁡q​(x,t)\nabla\log q(x,t).

Notice that the evolution of q⁡(x,t)q(x,t) is governed by the same Fokker-Planck equation:

∂q⁡(x,t)∂t=−∇[μF(x)q(x,t)−μkBT∇q(x,t)].\frac{\partial q(x,t)}{\partial t}=-\nabla[\mu F(x)q(x,t)-\mu k_{B}T\nabla q(x,t)]. (S15)

We substitute sθ​(x,τ−t)=∇log⁡q​(x,t)s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)=\nabla\log q(x,t) into Eq. (S8).

Δ​st​a=\displaystyle\Delta s_{ta}= Δ​ss​y​s+kB​∫0τsθ​(x,τ−t)⊤∘𝑑x\displaystyle\Delta s_{sys}+k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)^{\top}\circ dx (S16)
+μkB∫0τ[−F(x)⊤sθ(x,τ−t)+kBT||sθ(x,τ−t)||2+kBT∇⋅sθ(x,τ−t)−∇⋅F(x)]dt\displaystyle+\mu k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}[-F(x)^{\top}s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)+k_{B}T||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)||^{2}+k_{B}T\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)-\nabla\cdot F(x)]dt
=\displaystyle= Δ​ss​y​s+kB​∫0τ[∇log⁡q​(x,t)]⊤∘𝑑x\displaystyle\Delta s_{sys}+k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}[\nabla\log q(x,t)]^{\top}\circ dx
+μkB∫0τ[−F(x)⊤∇logq(x,t)+kBT||∇logq(x,t)||2+kBT∇2logq(x,t)−∇⋅F(x)]dt\displaystyle+\mu k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}[-F(x)^{\top}\nabla\log q(x,t)+k_{B}T||\nabla\log q(x,t)||^{2}+k_{B}T\nabla^{2}\log q(x,t)-\nabla\cdot F(x)]dt
=\displaystyle= Δ​ss​y​s+kB​∫0τ[∇log⁡q​(x,t)]⊤∘𝑑x\displaystyle\Delta s_{sys}+k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}[\nabla\log q(x,t)]^{\top}\circ dx
−kB∫0τ1q⁡(x,t)∇[μF(x)q(x,t)−μkBT∇q(x,t)]dt\displaystyle-k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\frac{1}{q(x,t)}\nabla[\mu F(x)q(x,t)-\mu k_{B}T\nabla q(x,t)]dt
=\displaystyle= Δ​ss​y​s+kB​∫0τ∂μlog⁡q⁡(x,t)∘d​xμ,\displaystyle\Delta s_{sys}+k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\partial_{\mu}\log q(x,t)\circ dx^{\mu},

where the last equality uses the Fokker-Planck equation. Using the second equality of Eq. (S9), we can further express the fluctuating TAEP as

Δ​st​a=kB​∫0τ∂μlog⁡q⁡(x,t)p⁡(x,t)∘d​xμ.\Delta s_{ta}=k_{B}\int_{0}^{\tau}\partial_{\mu}\log\frac{q(x,t)}{p(x,t)}\circ dx^{\mu}. (S17)

Then it follows that the average TAEP rate is given by

d​St​ad​t=kB​∫𝒥μ​(x,t)​∂μlog⁡q⁡(x,t)p⁡(x,t)​𝑑x,\frac{dS_{ta}}{dt}=k_{B}\int\mathcal{J}^{\mu}(x,t)\partial_{\mu}\log\frac{q(x,t)}{p(x,t)}dx, (S18)

where 𝒥≔(p,J)\mathcal{J}\coloneq(p,J).

Using integration by parts and assuming that the boundary term vanishes, Eq. (S18) can be alternatively written as the derivative of a KL divergence:

d​St​ad​t=−kBdd​tDK​L[p(x,t)||q(x,t)],\frac{dS_{ta}}{dt}=-k_{B}\frac{d}{dt}D_{KL}[p(x,t)||q(x,t)], (S19)

which is known to be non-negative [6]. Intuitively, p⁡(x,t)p(x,t) and q⁡(x,t)q(x,t) both converge to the stationary distribution in the forward process, and thus their KL divergence decreases.

IV Relation between mean and variance constrained by fluctuation theorem

Theorem 1.

Let (Xn)n≥1(X_{n})_{n\geq 1} be a sequence of real-valued random variables satisfying the integral fluctuation theorem

𝔼⁡[e−Xn]=1\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{-X_{n}}\right]=1

for every nn. Suppose also that

𝔼⁡[Xn]⟶0.\mathbb{E}[X_{n}]\longrightarrow 0.

Assume moreover that the family {Xn2}n≥1\{X_{n}^{2}\}_{n\geq 1} is uniformly integrable, i.e.

limK→∞supn𝔼[Xn2𝟏{|Xn|>K}]=0.\lim_{K\to\infty}\sup_{n}\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n}|>K\}}\right]=0.

Then

Var⁡(Xn)⟶0.\operatorname{Var}(X_{n})\longrightarrow 0.
Proof.

Define

g⁡(x)=x+e−x−1.g(x)=x+e^{-x}-1.

By the elementary inequality

e−x≥1−x,e^{-x}\geq 1-x,

we have

g⁡(x)≥0g(x)\geq 0

for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Moreover, equality holds if and only if x=0x=0.

Using the fluctuation theorem condition,

𝔼⁡[e−Xn]=1,\mathbb{E}[e^{-X_{n}}]=1,

we get

𝔼⁡[g⁡(Xn)]=𝔼⁡[Xn]+𝔼⁡[e−Xn]−1=𝔼⁡[Xn].\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n})]=\mathbb{E}[X_{n}]+\mathbb{E}[e^{-X_{n}}]-1=\mathbb{E}[X_{n}].

Therefore,

𝔼⁡[g⁡(Xn)]⟶0.\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n})]\longrightarrow 0.

We first show that Xn→0X_{n}\to 0 in probability. Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0. Since gg is continuous, strictly positive on the set

{x:|x|≥ε},\{x:|x|\geq\varepsilon\},

and satisfies g⁡(x)→∞g(x)\to\infty as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty, the number

cε:=inf|x|≥εg⁡(x)c_{\varepsilon}:=\inf_{|x|\geq\varepsilon}g(x)

is strictly positive. Hence

g(Xn)≥cε𝟏{|Xn|≥ε}.g(X_{n})\geq c_{\varepsilon}\mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n}|\geq\varepsilon\}}.

Taking expectations gives

cε​ℙ​(|Xn|≥ε)≤𝔼⁡[g⁡(Xn)].c_{\varepsilon}\mathbb{P}(|X_{n}|\geq\varepsilon)\leq\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n})].

Since 𝔼⁡[g⁡(Xn)]→0\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n})]\to 0, it follows that

ℙ⁡(|Xn|≥ε)→0.\mathbb{P}(|X_{n}|\geq\varepsilon)\to 0.

Thus

Xn→0X_{n}\to 0

in probability.

We now upgrade convergence in probability to convergence in L2L^{2}. By uniform integrability of {Xn2}\{X_{n}^{2}\}, for every η>0\eta>0 there exists K>0K>0 such that

supn𝔼[Xn2𝟏{|Xn|>K}]<η.\sup_{n}\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n}|>K\}}\right]<\eta.

Fix also δ>0\delta>0. Decompose

𝔼[Xn2]=𝔼[Xn2𝟏{|Xn|≤δ}]+𝔼[Xn2𝟏{δ<|Xn|≤K}]+𝔼[Xn2𝟏{|Xn|>K}].\mathbb{E}[X_{n}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n}|\leq\delta\}}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{\delta<|X_{n}|\leq K\}}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n}|>K\}}\right].

The three terms are bounded as follows:

𝔼[Xn2𝟏{|Xn|≤δ}]≤δ2,\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n}|\leq\delta\}}\right]\leq\delta^{2},
𝔼[Xn2𝟏{δ<|Xn|≤K}]≤K2ℙ(|Xn|>δ),\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{\delta<|X_{n}|\leq K\}}\right]\leq K^{2}\mathbb{P}(|X_{n}|>\delta),

and

𝔼[Xn2𝟏{|Xn|>K}]<η.\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n}|>K\}}\right]<\eta.

Therefore

𝔼⁡[Xn2]≤δ2+K2​ℙ​(|Xn|>δ)+η.\mathbb{E}[X_{n}^{2}]\leq\delta^{2}+K^{2}\mathbb{P}(|X_{n}|>\delta)+\eta.

Taking lim supn→∞\limsup_{n\to\infty} and using Xn→0X_{n}\to 0 in probability, we obtain

lim supn→∞𝔼⁡[Xn2]≤δ2+η.\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[X_{n}^{2}]\leq\delta^{2}+\eta.

Since δ>0\delta>0 and η>0\eta>0 are arbitrary,

𝔼⁡[Xn2]→0.\mathbb{E}[X_{n}^{2}]\to 0.

Finally,

Var⁡(Xn)=𝔼⁡[Xn2]−(𝔼⁡[Xn])2.\operatorname{Var}(X_{n})=\mathbb{E}[X_{n}^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[X_{n}])^{2}.

We have shown that 𝔼⁡[Xn2]→0\mathbb{E}[X_{n}^{2}]\to 0, and by assumption 𝔼⁡[Xn]→0\mathbb{E}[X_{n}]\to 0. Hence

Var⁡(Xn)→0.\operatorname{Var}(X_{n})\to 0.

∎

V Variance of per-trajectory and per-sample loss

In practice, the score-matching objective, Eq. (), is usually decomposed into the per-sample loss as follows.

ℒS​M​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{SM}(\theta) =𝔼x0∼p⁡(x,0)​[ℒD​S​M​(θ,x0)]+c​o​n​s​t.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}\sim p(x,0)}[\mathcal{L}_{DSM}(\theta,x_{0})]+const. (S20)
ℒD​S​M​(θ,x0)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{DSM}(\theta,x_{0}) ≔∫0τ⟨‖sθ​(x,τ−t)−∇log⁡p​(x,t|x0)‖2⟩x∼p⁡(x,t|x0)​dt,\displaystyle\coloneq\int_{0}^{\tau}\langle||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)-\nabla\log p(x,t|x_{0})||^{2}\rangle_{x\sim p(x,t|x_{0})}dt,

which is known as the denoising score-matching objective [15]. In particular, when F⁡(x)F(x) is a linear function in xx, as in variance-exploding and variance-preserving settings, the conditional score ∇log⁡p​(x,t|x0)\nabla\log p(x,t|x_{0}) is proportional to the corrupting noise added to the sample. People usually use the Monte Carlo method to estimate the per-sample loss and minimize it using optimizers.

We note that, up to constants, the per-sample loss is proportional to the average of the trajectory TAEP conditioned on the sample:

⟨Δst​a[x([t])]|x(0)=x0⟩\displaystyle\langle\Delta s_{ta}[x([t])]|x(0)=x_{0}\rangle (S21)
=\displaystyle= μkB2T∫0τ∫p(x,t|x0)[||sθ(x,τ−t)||2+2∇⋅sθ(x,τ−t)]dxdt+const.\displaystyle\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}\int p(x,t|x_{0})[||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)||^{2}+2\nabla\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)]dxdt+const.
=\displaystyle= μkB2T∫0τ∫p(x,t|x0)[||sθ(x,τ−t)||2−2∇logp(x,t|x0)⋅sθ(x,τ−t)]dxdt+const.\displaystyle\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}\int p(x,t|x_{0})[||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)||^{2}-2\nabla\log p(x,t|x_{0})\cdot s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)]dxdt+const.
=\displaystyle= μ​kB2​T​∫0τ∫p⁡(x,t|x0)​‖sθ​(x,τ−t)−∇log⁡p​(x,t|x0)‖2​dx​dt+c​o​n​s​t.\displaystyle\mu k_{B}^{2}T\int_{0}^{\tau}\int p(x,t|x_{0})||s_{\theta}(x,\tau-t)-\nabla\log p(x,t|x_{0})||^{2}dxdt+const.
=\displaystyle= μ​kB2​T​ℒD​S​M​(θ,x0)+c​o​n​s​t.\displaystyle\mu k_{B}^{2}T\mathcal{L}_{DSM}(\theta,x_{0})+const.

Treating the trajectories starting from the same sample as a group, the variance of the TAEP can be decomposed into the variance of group means and the within-group variance:

Var​(Δ​st​a)=(μ​kB2​T)2​Var​[ℒD​S​M​(θ,x0)]+𝔼⁡[Var​(Δ​st​a|x⁡(0)=x0)].\text{Var}(\Delta s_{ta})=(\mu k_{B}^{2}T)^{2}\text{Var}[\mathcal{L}_{DSM}(\theta,x_{0})]+\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(\Delta s_{ta}|x(0)=x_{0})]. (S22)

We numerically compare the magnitudes of these two components throughout the training process (Fig. S1), indicating that the per-sample loss variance is the dominant component of the per-trajectory loss variance.
